Alder Row does not need a bigger catalogue before it needs a clearer way to borrow. Our tool library began in March 2026 with neighbours sharing things they already owned. This autumn note explains what the register records, what the pictures show, and where we need help. It is an invitation to take part, not a claim that every household needs the same tools. We want a new volunteer to understand the routine before agreeing to a shift, and a borrower to know what happens when an item comes back.

## Start with what the register records

Our [borrowing register](https://library.example.org/report?period=autumn#loans) records **40 participating households and 120 completed loans** between March and September 2026. Those are different measures: a household can borrow more than once, and a completed loan is not the same thing as a person reached. We have not measured how many purchases were avoided, so we are not turning the loan count into a savings claim. The useful point is smaller and more practical. The register lets the next volunteer see which item left the shelf, when it is due back, and whether its return has been recorded. That makes the handover easier to follow without relying on someone remembering a conversation.

[PICTURE 1: register.png]

## Make the shelf easy to read

The [shelf map](https://library.example.org/shelves) groups items by the job they help with rather than by who donated them. A borrower should be able to find the place for a drill without knowing the history of the drill. The labels in the supplied photograph match the names in the catalogue. We want to keep that connection when a shelf is moved or an item is replaced. A tidy photograph is useful for explaining the system, but it does not prove that the system stays tidy every day. Volunteers still need to check the label against the catalogue and record any difference before offering an item to the next borrower.

[PICTURE 2: shelf-map.png]

## Show the return check

Our [return checklist](https://library.example.org/returns) asks the volunteer to compare the returned item with its catalogue entry, note visible damage, and record anything that needs a closer look. This is a record of the return, not a promise about technical condition. A volunteer who is unsure should flag the item for review rather than reassure the next borrower without evidence. The photograph of the return desk is there to make the sequence easy to recognize. It should sit beside these instructions, where someone learning the job can connect the words with the place they will actually use. Clear records help the next shift understand what happened.

[PICTURE 3: return-desk.jpg]

## Describe a repair without claiming a rescue

The [repair log](https://library.example.org/repairs) distinguishes an issue that has been reported from work that has been finished. We should keep that distinction in public updates too. A photograph of an item on the bench does not tell us whether it is ready to lend again. Before changing its status, the volunteer needs the completed record and the decision recorded by the person doing the check. This may sound like a small wording choice, but it changes what a borrower can reasonably expect. We can show work in progress without making it look finished. The supplied repair photo belongs here, next to the explanation of those different states.

[PICTURE 4: repair-bench.jpg]

## Make a volunteer shift understandable

The [volunteer guide](https://library.example.org/volunteer) describes opening the register, checking expected returns, helping a borrower find an item, and leaving notes for the next shift. We need more people willing to learn that routine. We are not attaching a fixed weekly time commitment to this invitation because the notes do not give one. Someone considering a shift should be able to ask what the work involves and what support is available before saying yes. The supplied rota image explains how shifts are organized, but it contains no confirmed vacancies or dates in this brief. We should not invent those details to make the invitation look more complete.

[PICTURE 5: rota.png]

## Keep the practical questions together

The [questions page](https://library.example.org/questions) is the place for borrowing arrangements and the steps to take when a return is late or an item cannot be found. Those details should remain easy to reach from this article rather than being scattered across a series of unrelated posts. The accompanying process chart shows the route from a question to a recorded answer. It is an explanation of the routine, not a measurement of response speed. If a reader needs an answer the page does not contain, we should add the question to the next review instead of pretending that every situation is already covered by the current instructions.

[PICTURE 6: questions-flow.png]

## Give people one clear next step

The [joining page](https://library.example.org/join) is the next step for a neighbour who wants to volunteer or ask about borrowing. We should use the words that describe that destination so readers know what they will open. There is no reason to make them guess whether a link leads to a form, a report or another article. The supplied overview diagram can help explain how the register, shelves and return desk fit together. It should follow the invitation, where it reinforces the whole routine. We are asking people to understand and consider the work, not claiming that reading this article signs them up for anything.

[PICTURE 7: overview.png]

## Keep the invitation grounded

The final picture is the library entrance, included so a new volunteer can recognize the place described in these notes. We have not supplied opening hours, a street address or a date for an introductory session, so this article does not invent them. Those practical details need to come from the team before the final public version. For now, the article can still explain the purpose and routine, preserve the recorded totals, and point to the joining page already supplied. A useful invitation gives people enough information to decide what to ask next while leaving unanswered questions visible for the person preparing the final draft.
